item.title: My impressions of WAIC 2026: robots, AI for Science, and the Chinese perspective on the future of AI.
item.description:
Hello, Habr! My name is Alena, and I do research in artificial intelligence and genomics at AIRI. In July, I had the opportunity to attend the World Artificial Intelligence Conference 2026 in Shanghai — one of the largest global platforms bringing together scientific research, industrial developments, and a wide variety of practical AI applications. The trip left me with a wealth of impressions that I want to share with you.

item.title: The non-obvious influence of artificial intelligence on human intelligence.
item.description:
I have repeatedly witnessed a small child of 2–3 years old playing on a smartphone while the parent nearby carefreely minds their own business. I won't talk about the fact that such a child is highly likely to experience problems with vision, learning ability, and thinking — that varies individually. Right now, I am observing a problem that, in my opinion, is more global and serious.

Not long ago, artificial intelligence models could barely write coherent text. And quite recently, the release of one of the latest versions was postponed due to a threat to the computer security of US banks. But literally within a few months, it (AI) became so good that people began to be laid off by the thousands: programmers, designers, secretaries, writers, translators, and many others. This is what is replacing humans in a number of employment sectors. And those who remain or have remained complain that the work has ceased to be creative and enjoyable.

Many college graduates in developed countries cannot find work because artificial intelligence is quite successfully handling the work of entry-level specialists. The only advice given to young graduates is that they must possess good skills in working with artificial intelligence.

What impact does artificial intelligence have on the mental sphere?

Researchers from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology conducted an interesting experiment in which they asked participants to write an essay.

The participants were divided into three groups. One used artificial intelligence as a helper, another used a search engine, and the third used only their own mental abilities.

Read more

item.title: Can AI independently understand the Siemens TIA Portal project? Experience developing OpennessLLM
item.description:
When I first started using language models in my work with TIA Portal, everything seemed quite familiar. You copy a snippet of SCL code into the chat, describe the task, and receive an explanation or a ready-made function. Sometimes the result can be used almost unchanged, other times you have to spend a long time clarifying the context.

But fairly quickly, I ran into an obvious limitation: the model only sees what I show it.

If the error is in a single block, that might be sufficient. In a real project, things are usually more complex. One signal is generated in one place, checked in another, saved in a DB, then participates in several conditions and ultimately affects the operation of a completely different part of the program.

To get a useful answer, you have to manually search for related blocks, copy them into the chat, explain the project structure, pass on compiler messages, and then return to TIA Portal for the next piece of information.

At some point, a simple question occurred to me: why should the model have to wait for me to bring it the next block? Could it be given the ability to independently study the TIA Portal project, find the necessary code, verify its assumptions, and prepare changes?

That is how OpennessLLM came about.

Read more

item.title: "Why use a platform when Kafka exists?" I'll answer honestly, including the part where you're right.
item.description:
Hello, Habr! My name is Viktor Ovchinnikov, I lead the product direction "Integration Platform" at Diasoft. The very same Digital Q.Integration that you have every right not to buy.

Under each of my articles, the same comment appears. The words differ, but the meaning is the same: why is an integration platform needed at all if there is Kafka, a message broker? One service put a message, the other took it. What, in fact, is the problem?

Previously, I replied to each one in the comments, then I realized it's easier to answer everyone at once. And also to admit an unpleasant thing: in a considerable number of cases, this comment is justified. The good news is that over the years of conversations with colleagues from other companies, I have accumulated a decent collection of objections against myself. These are architects, analysts, development managers – people who do not sell the platform. I will retell some of these conversations here, sometimes even verbatim.

Next will be about where the boundary between the broker and the platform lies, why it is so difficult to feel it, why the real reason for "self-writing" is not technical at all, and what AI has changed in this whole story. Regarding the last point, spoiler: nothing good.

Read more

item.title: DevOps engineer and AI dive into business tasks with both feet.
item.description:
209 thousand product names across 150 offices are recorded differently, and a regular join matches at most 1% of them. Data engineer Dmitry Dunaev at the Slerom Evening School showed how to clean up this mess using LLM, embeddings, and fuzzy search, while also saving managers from 5-minute calls from an endless call list.

Out of the 15 models tested, only one achieved the right balance of criteria. Which one exactly and why — we break it down in the talk summary, along with a checklist for when building an agent is worth it and when it's better to save money.

item.title: Local LLM migration Vertica2Trino. How to bring to working state if the model cannot handle it.
item.description:
Hi, this is the BI development team of the commercial department: Alexey Dubinets and Pavel Bespalov. 

In the article, we will tell how we built a migration pipeline for our data marts using a local LLM. 

Let me clarify right away: this is not a story about how we gave it to Codex or Claude Code, wrote a skill, and got a magical result. We will show the engineering part of the task: where the local model fails, which naive solutions don't work, and what we had to build around it to make the translation reproducible.

item.title: [Translation] AI was used to verify the most complex mathematical proof to date.
item.description:
An important milestone in mathematical research using AI was the example of the team from the company Axiom Math, which for the first time automatically verified the proof of a theorem concerning prime numbers — commonly known as the "theorem 246" — using its own artificial intelligence system, AxiomProver.

In formal verification, mathematicians task a computer with checking a machine-readable version of the proof. This process does not guarantee 100% correctness of the proof, as a recent demonstration showed, during which it was revealed that an error in the method could lead to a false confirmation of an AI-generated proof. Nevertheless, this computational method brings the approval of a proof with the help of AI as close to reality as possible.

This confirmation formalizes an important breakthrough in number theory. Beyond this specific proof, it demonstrates how automated AI-assisted verification could be used in the future to ensure the correctness of AI-generated computer code, which will soon become the foundation of software worldwide.

Read more

item.title: Modders hacked DLSS 5 and stuffed it into everything — from Skyrim to GTA San Andreas.
item.description:
Sometimes something super-mega-secret leaks out not through a leak, but simply because someone forgot to remove one file from the build. Oh well, they forgot, it happens to everyone.

That's exactly what happened last week with DLSS 5 – a controversial thing from Nvidia. There was no official announcement, but there was an early version of the game NBA 2K27, which contained an inconspicuous DLL file nvngx_dlssnr.dll weighing 158 megabytes... and off it went.

Within days, modders had applied the neural network render to a good three dozen games, from Cyberpunk 2077 to GTA San Andreas, which is already twenty years old (though the remaster is a bit younger).

If you've been following DLSS 5 since March, you remember all those memes and hate. Let's try to figure out what happened, how it works technically, what the tests show, and why people are still arguing about the fate of the gaming industry. I'll also throw in some pictures and videos, because this is one of those cases where seeing once is better than reading a hundred times.

Read more

item.title: The agents completed the task. Why is the test still failed?
item.description:
Suppose you have several AI agents. One processes a ticket, the second modifies code, the third runs tests, the fourth prepares a release.

The task is resolved, tests are green, the artifact is built. The success_rate metric shows success.

Time to celebrate?

Not necessarily. The agents might have done the same work multiple times, violated the order of operations, simultaneously grabbed a shared resource, or accidentally achieved the correct result through an invalid sequence of actions.

The final state is correct. The process — not.

This is exactly the problem that CoCoBench — a new benchmark for evaluating coordination of multiple AI agents — tries to measure. It was developed by researchers from Nanjing University, Tsinghua, and AgiBot.

The main idea of the research is useful far beyond robotics:

How bad is it?

item.title: Mobile audio guide or how I made an app for self-guided city walks
item.description:
I continue to talk about the results of my small automation tools, or about the fact that today almost anyone can make for themselves the application they need.

I was once walking through the city alleys. Old buildings full of stories. And I absolutely love history. Whose house it was, when it was built, who lived there, and what else interesting. There's no plaque on the facade, no tour guide materializes nearby. Constantly pulling out your phone, searching the internet, opening several sites — that's quite a chore. You could take a photo of the building and figure it out later. "Later" almost never comes.

That's how the idea for Yerick City Explorer was born — an Android app for self-guided city walks.

Read more

item.title: AI detectors. Are we on the path to a world of dystopias?
item.description:
Introduction. No neural networks were used in the writing of this opus.

Setup. I sometimes share my expert observations on a topic I have been involved with for over 10 years. This includes occasionally using neural networks for 2 tasks: finding new information that I might have missed, and final text processing before publication to make complex text more reader-friendly.

The other day, on one platform, moderators removed an article with the justification "Generated text." And when I sent a request to technical support, 3 other publications that had garnered over 50 thousand views were also banned.

Journalists, representatives of research institutes, and government agencies have reached out to me for permission to use these materials. In other words, there seems to be no issue regarding the level of expertise, but the AI detector somehow fell short... And I became curious to take a more professional look at this beast.

From a logical standpoint, it's important to agree at the very start on what we aim to achieve through the total use of AI detectors. Options: 1. That authors write themselves. Period! 2. To avoid generating a billion units of content! 3. To...?

And here I ask myself: what is important for me to get from an article/book/essay? And I answer myself: enjoyment from reading / new important information / a new interesting author or expert to look into. Whether neural networks were used or not is completely unimportant. "Liked/disliked — that's the main criterion!"

Read more

item.title: Claude Code this week: /resume in desktop, session launch from phone, and subagents' own memory
item.description:
On August 29, Anthropic sent out a weekly digest on Claude Code. Summary in Russian: /resume picks up a terminal session in the desktop application, a session on your own machine can be launched from a phone via Remote Control, a subagent can be given its own memory between sessions using the memory line in frontmatter, and /color and /rename help distinguish multiple open terminals. Plus versions 2.1.243–2.1.248: --restricted mode, automatic bug report, editing auto-mode rules from /permissions, hour-long prompt cache, zstd-compressed CLI binary, and fixed desktop sessions.
